# Demo — real lecture clip → slides (PDF + PPTX)

This folder proves SlideSnap works on **real footage**, not just the
synthetic corpus: a 100 s slice of Stanford CS231n Lecture 1
(Justin Johnson, 4/4/2017, YouTube `vT1JzLTH4G4`, CC-BY) covering
`t=40 s → t=140 s` (speaker intro → "Welcome to CS231n" photo slide).

## Input

- `cs231n_clip.mp4` — 100 s, 720p, MPEG-4 (30 MB). Sliced with
  `ffmpeg -ss 40 -t 100` from the lecture; no other processing.

## Outputs (generated by the committed pipeline, no hand edits)

- `slides.pdf` / `slides.pptx` — the extracted deck (run
  `python -m slidesnap demo/cs231n_clip.mp4 --out <dir>` to reproduce).
- `keyframes.png` — rectified keyframe grid from `debug/`.
- `scores.csv` — per-pair diff/hist/SSIM log for the clip.

## What the demo shows (measured, uncherry-picked)

- Detection: 3 segments → changes at 10.5 s / 12.0 s (clip-relative).
  The 12.0 s cut is a **real slide change** (speaker → photo slide) that the
  old neighbourhood-count burst mask vetoed (it sat next to motion); the
  consecutive-run mask (`BURST_MIN_RUN=3`) detects it.
- Non-slide filter: the 2 speaker keyframes drop
  (4 words/yspread 0.55, 3 words/0.46 — both under the
  `<5 words AND <0.75 spread` cut); the photo slide keeps
  (9+ words, spread 0.96).
- Dedup near-dup threshold: exact photo re-shows SSIM 0.9918 and the
  eyeball-graphics build 0.951 collapse; speaker-vs-speaker 0.9317 does not
  (`DEDUP_NEAR_DUP_SSIM=0.94`).
- OCR (RapidOCR, CPU): photo slide reads "Welcome to CS231n",
  "TheEuropeanCameraoftheYear1983.", footer names/date; fine print stays
  noisy — expected at 720p with overlaid watermarks.
- PDF page is full **color** (photo slides need it); PPTX carries the same
  image plus OCR text in the speaker notes.

## Limits this demo exposes (honest)

- The clip holds only ~2 distinct slides in 100 s, so it exercises the
  speaker-vs-slide split more than slide-change recall.
- Photo slides defeat Tesseract-style word boxes on fine print; text-layer
  recall on dense photo montages is partial.
- Source: Stanford CS231n (2017), used for evaluation illustration only.
